title: Career discovery
description: Exploring the world of work through play, curiosity and research, without choosing too early. Deeper exploration and real pathways from 13 to 17.

nodes.title: Role play
nodes.description: Pretend to do different jobs through play.

nodes.title: Jobs around us
nodes.description: Notice the people who work in your community.

nodes.title: Career families
nodes.description: Explore the big families of jobs.

nodes.title: Strengths and interests
nodes.description: Notice what you enjoy and what you are good at.

nodes.title: Real-world research
nodes.description: Find out about jobs by researching and asking people.

nodes.title: Pathways

nodes.description: Make a flexible plan and build evidence like a CV and portfolio.

competencies.title: Can name 20 different jobs and what they do
Can describe own strengths and interests
Can interview someone about their work
Can explain skills that are useful in many jobs
Can explain apprenticeship, college and university routes
Can write a simple CV and portfolio
Knows how to behave safely and professionally at a workplace

items.subject: role play
items.title: Pretend jobs
steps: 🧸 Be a vet: check a teddy gently.
🍳 Be a chef: stir a pretend soup.
🚒 Be a firefighter: ring the bell!
🔧 Be a mechanic: fix a toy car.
🏪 Be a shopkeeper: sell toys.
💬 Which job was the most fun?

hazards: Real kitchen tools can be sharp or hot
safety.notes: Use toys or safe, cold, unbreakable items only. No real knives or stoves.

basic.description: Use things from home as props.

better.description: Make hats, badges and a cardboard shop.

materials: Toy doctor kit or toy tools
advanced.description: Add a simple toy kit for one job.

substitutions.use: A scarf as a bandage and a spoon as a stethoscope

items.adultNote: Offer every job to every child. Avoid "that's a boy's job" or "girl's job" - any child can do any job.

items.subject: community helpers
items.title: Jobs all around us
items.summary: Many people do jobs that help us every day.
steps: 👩‍🌾 A farmer grows food.
🧑‍🍳 A chef cooks meals.
🧑‍🔧 A mechanic fixes cars and bikes.
🧑‍⚕️ A nurse looks after sick people.
🧑‍🏫 A teacher helps us learn.
🧑‍🚒 A firefighter keeps us safe.
✏️ Draw someone you have seen working.

check.question: Who grows food?
check.explain: Yes! Farmers grow food for all of us.

items.subject: career families
items.title: Whose tool is it?
items.summary: Every job has special tools. Can you match them?
steps: 🩺 Stethoscope - who uses it?
🥄 Whisk - who uses it?
🔧 Spanner - who uses it?
🎨 Paintbrush - who uses it?
🔬 Microscope - who uses it?
🧱 Trowel - who uses it?

check.question: 🩺 is used by a...
check.explain: Yes! It helps them listen to your heart.

check.question: 🔧 is used by a...
check.explain: Yes! Mechanics use spanners to turn nuts and bolts.

items.subject: community helpers
items.title: Job detective
items.summary: Be a detective and spot people at work.
steps: Go for a walk with an adult, or look at a picture book or newspaper.
Spot as many jobs as you can: drivers, shop workers, builders, gardeners.
Make a tally for each job you spot.
Pick one job. What tools did they use? What problem do they solve?
Draw your favourite and write one question you would ask that worker.
items.adultNote: Stay together and do not disturb people while they work. If going out is hard, use books, TV or a window.

items.subject: career families
items.title: The 16 career families
items.summary: Jobs come in big families. You do not need to choose one now - just explore!
steps: Medicine 🩺 and science 🔬: health and discovering how things work.
Engineering ⚙️ and technology 💻: designing machines, buildings, computers and code.
Finance 💰 and business 🏪: money, shops and companies.
Agriculture 🌾: growing food and caring for farm animals.
Skilled trades 🔧: plumbers, electricians, mechanics, carpenters.
Hospitality 🍽️: cooking, hotels and looking after visitors.
Arts 🎭 and design 🎨: music, acting, drawing, fashion and buildings.
Law ⚖️, education 🧑‍🏫, public service 🚒 and research 📚.
Entrepreneurship 🚀: starting your own business or project.
Pick three families you want to find out more about.

items.subject: self-knowledge
items.title: What do I enjoy? What am I good at?
items.summary: Your interests and strengths change as you grow. Let's notice them now.
steps: Write 5 things you enjoy doing.
Write 5 things you are good at (ask family to help!).
Circle things that are on both lists.
Do you like working with people, things, ideas, animals or nature?
Find two career families that use your circled strengths.
Remember: this is for exploring, not choosing. Do it again next year!
items.adultNote: Interests should widen options, not narrow them. Encourage trying things outside the child's comfort zone.

items.subject: research
items.title: A day in the life
items.summary: Find out what a worker really does all day.
steps: Pick a job you are curious about.
Find out: what time do they start? Where do they work? What tools do they use?
Use a library book, a free careers website or ask an adult who knows the job.
Draw a timeline of their day from morning to evening.
Add: what is the best part of the job? What is hard?

items.subject: career families
items.title: Every job solves a problem
items.summary: Jobs exist because people have problems and needs.
steps: A plumber solves leaks and gets clean water to us.
A data scientist finds patterns that help people make decisions.
A farmer solves the problem of feeding people.
A designer solves the problem of making things easy and beautiful to use.
Think of a problem you notice. Which jobs help solve it?
Make a "problem → job" chart with 5 examples.

check.question: Which job solves the problem of a leaking pipe?
check.explain: Yes! Plumbers fix leaks and water systems.

items.subject: research
items.title: Interview a worker
items.summary: Ask someone about their job to learn things no book will tell you.
steps: With an adult, choose someone known to your family: a relative, neighbour or family friend.
Prepare 8 questions, for example: How did you get this job? What do you do each day? What do you wish you had known at my age?
Ask permission to take notes.
Listen carefully and ask follow-up questions.
Thank them, and send a thank-you note.
Write a one-page summary of what you learned.
items.adultNote: Arrange the interview yourself and stay present or nearby. A phone or video call is fine.

items.subject: skills
items.title: Skills that travel
items.summary: Some skills help in almost every job. They go with you wherever you work.
steps: Communication: speaking, writing and listening clearly.
Teamwork: working well with others.
Problem-solving: working out what is wrong and trying solutions.
Reliability: being on time and doing what you said.
Digital skills: using computers and phones well and safely.
Learning to learn: picking up new skills when things change.
For each skill, write one example of when you used it at home.

check.question: Which skill is useful in almost every job?

items.subject: work readiness
items.title: First day of work experience
items.summary: You are starting a short work placement. What do you do?
steps: Read each situation.
Choose the best action.
Think about safety and professional behaviour.

safety.notes: A pretend scenario about workplace behaviour and safety.

simulation.scenario: It is your first morning of work experience at a small workshop.

options.text: Arrive on time, introduce yourself and ask who to report to
options.feedback: Great start. Being on time shows reliability.

options.text: Start using the machines to look helpful
options.feedback: Never use equipment before training and permission.

steps.prompt: Your supervisor gives a safety briefing. What do you do?

options.text: Listen carefully, ask questions and follow the rules, including protective equipment
Skip it - you already know about safety
options.feedback: Every workplace has its own risks. Always listen.

steps.prompt: Someone asks you to do something that seems unsafe.

options.text: Politely say no and tell your supervisor or a trusted adult
options.feedback: Exactly right. You can always refuse unsafe work.

options.text: Do it so you do not upset anyone
options.feedback: Your safety comes first. Young workers should never do unsafe tasks.

options.text: Ask what you can help with next
options.feedback: Excellent. Showing initiative makes a strong impression.
Ask for the next task instead.

items.subject: pathways
items.title: Many paths into work
items.summary: There is no single right route. Learn about the main pathways and how they connect.
steps: Apprenticeships: learn on the job, earn money and get a qualification (common in trades, engineering, business and care).
Vocational or technical college: practical courses for specific skills.
University: degrees for professions like medicine, law, research and teaching, and many others.
Starting a business or freelancing: create your own work.
Volunteering, internships and part-time jobs build experience.
Paths can change. Many people switch careers or study later in life.
For two careers you are curious about, map the possible routes, time and cost. Find free or funded options where you live.

check.question: An apprenticeship lets you...
options: learn and earn at the same time
check.explain: Yes. Apprentices work and train together.

items.adultNote: Routes, costs and funding vary by country. Help the child find official careers guidance for your area.

items.subject: real-world exploration
items.title: Plan a job shadow
items.summary: Spend time watching someone at work to see what the job is really like.
steps: Choose a job you want to understand better.
With an adult, find a known person or organisation who might let you shadow them.
Write a polite request explaining what you hope to learn.
Agree the details: date, times, place, what to wear, safety rules and who is responsible for you.
On the day: observe, ask questions, take notes and follow all safety instructions.
Afterwards, write a reflection: what surprised you? Would you like to try this work?
Send a thank-you message.

hazards: Being in unfamiliar places with unfamiliar adults
safety.notes: An adult arranges and approves the placement and knows where the young person is. Only observe, unless trained and permitted. Follow the workplace's safety rules and local laws on young workers.

basic.description: A virtual shadow: a worker talks you through their day and shows their workplace on a call.

better.description: Half a day observing a family friend at work.

materials: Formal placement arranged with an organisation
advanced.description: A one-week work-experience placement with a supervisor and safety induction.

substitutions.use: A phone or video call, or a documentary about the job
Volunteering with a community group alongside a parent

sources.title: Child labour and decent work for young people

items.adultNote: Check local laws about young people in workplaces and any required permissions or checks. Never pressure a young person to stay somewhere they feel unsafe.

items.subject: next steps
items.title: My first CV and portfolio
items.summary: Show what you can do: write a short CV and gather evidence from your Life Competency Passport.
steps: List your contact details (only share these with people you trust and real employers).
Write a 2-sentence profile about your interests and strengths.
List skills and competencies you have earned, with an example for each.
Add projects, volunteering, clubs and any jobs or responsibilities at home.
Build a portfolio: photos of things you made, writing, code, certificates.
Ask an adult to check spelling and give feedback.
Update it every few months.

safety.notes: Keep your address and phone number off public websites.

basic.description: Handwrite the CV and keep a paper portfolio in a folder.

better.description: Take photos of your work and type the CV in a free notes or document app.

advanced.description: Design a polished CV and a digital portfolio.

substitutions.use: A library or community centre printer

items.subject: entrepreneurship
items.title: Test a tiny business idea
items.summary: Entrepreneurs test ideas cheaply before spending lots of money. Try it!
steps: Spot a problem people have, such as plants that need watering while neighbours travel.
Describe your solution in one sentence.
Ask 5 people (known to you, with an adult) if they would use it and what they would pay.
Work out costs, price and how much you could earn.
Run a tiny test with family or friends for one or two weeks.
Record what worked and what did not. Change your idea and try again.

safety.notes: Keep customers to people your family knows. An adult helps with money and agreements.

basic.description: Plan the idea and survey people without selling anything.

materials: Simple materials for a product or service
better.description: Run a small test service for family and neighbours.

advanced.description: Run the test for a month and track all costs and income.

substitutions.use: A paper notebook with columns for money in and out

items.adultNote: Check any local rules on young people selling goods or services.

items.subject: community helpers
items.title: Thank a helper
items.summary: Many people help us every day. Let us make a thank-you picture for one of them!
steps: 🤔 Think of a helper: someone who brings letters, takes the rubbish, or helps at the shop.
🖍️ Draw a picture of them doing their job.
❤️ Add a big heart or a smiley face.
🗣️ Say what they do. A grown-up writes "thank you".
💌 Give it to them with your grown-up.

check.question: Who brings letters?
check.explain: Yes! Postal workers bring letters and parcels.

check.question: When someone helps us, we say...
check.explain: Yes! Saying thank you makes helpers happy.

items.adultNote: Choose a helper the child sees often. Show that any person can do any job. Always give the picture together; the child does not approach strangers alone.

items.subject: community helpers
items.title: Who helped make my breakfast?
items.summary: Lots of people help bring food to your table. Who are they?
steps: 👩‍🌾 A farmer grows the grain and the fruit.
🚚 A driver takes the food to the shop.
🛒 A shop worker puts it on the shelf.
🧑‍🍳 Someone at home makes the breakfast.
🙏 Say thank you to all of them!

check.question: Who grows food?
check.explain: Yes! Farmers grow food for all of us.

check.question: Who takes food to the shop?
check.explain: Yes! Drivers bring food from farms to shops.

items.adultNote: Use whatever your family eats. Show that farmers, drivers and cooks can be anyone. Point out the journey next time you shop together.

items.subject: community helpers
items.title: Who can help?
items.summary: Things go wrong in a busy day. Choose which worker has the right skills to help.
steps: Read the story.
Choose the worker who can help at each step.
Think: which of these jobs would you like to try?

safety.notes: A thinking game. No physical activity.

simulation.scenario: It is a busy day in your town. A few problems pop up. Who has the right skills?

steps.prompt: The water pipe under the kitchen sink is dripping. Who can fix it?

options.feedback: Yes! Plumbers fix pipes, taps and drains.
Bakers make bread and cakes. A plumber fixes pipes.

steps.prompt: Your neighbour's goat has a sore leg. Who can help?

options.feedback: Right. Vets are doctors for animals.
Tailors make and mend clothes. A vet cares for animals.
Pilots fly planes. A vet is the animal doctor.

steps.prompt: The bicycle chain keeps falling off. Who can help?

options.feedback: Yes! Mechanics know how machines work and fix them.
Teachers help us learn. A mechanic fixes bicycles, though a teacher could help you learn how!

steps.prompt: Can a girl or a boy grow up to do any of these jobs?

options.text: Yes, anyone can learn any of these jobs
options.feedback: That is right. Jobs need skills, and anyone can learn skills.

options.text: No, some jobs are only for some people
options.feedback: Every job here can be done by anyone who learns the skills.

items.adultNote: Swap in workers the child sees locally. Point out real people in your community who do these jobs.

items.subject: role play
items.title: Job charades
items.summary: Act out a job without words. Can your family guess what it is?
steps: Write or draw jobs on small papers: farmer, nurse, driver, cook, builder, singer.
Fold them and put them in a cup.
Pick one. Act it out with no talking!
Others guess the job.
When someone guesses, say one tool that worker uses.
Take turns until all the jobs are done.
items.adultNote: Include jobs from your area, such as fishers, shopkeepers, health workers or coders. Mix up who acts which job so every child sees that anyone can do any work.
